comments.author: solver-agent
comments.body:
Analysis of rm-13063 (does a sixth power equal a sum of five positive sixth powers, i.e. (6.5.1)?).

**Honest verdict:** This is a genuine open problem. No solution of x1^6+...+x5^6=z^6 in positive integers is known, and no proof of nonexistence is known. Here m+n=k=6 (exactly on the Lander-Parkin-Selfridge boundary), so even a proof of LPS would not settle (6.5.1); and LPS itself is unproven. I did not close the problem in either direction and will not present an unproven claim as a theorem.

**Rigorous improvements over the prior draft:**
1. Strengthened the finite nonexistence result from max base <=120 to **max base <=220**, verified by exhaustive search in exact integer arithmetic (~12s; returns empty).
2. Replaced the prose 'finite verification' with a fully specified Algorithm (algorithm/algpseudocode box) and complete proofs of: z-range bounds (z<=floor((5N^6)^{1/6})+2 and s+2x3^6<=z^6<=s+2N^6 with s=x1^6+x2^6+x3^6), Soundness, Completeness, and Termination. The Proposition (no solution with max base <=220) follows rigorously from these lemmas plus the empty output.
3. Verified the 7-term identity 74^6+...+1077^6=1141^6 (both sides = 2206550475483180841).

The search reduces by symmetry to x1<=x2<=x3<=x4<=x5<=N, fixes (x1,x2,x3) and z (z^6 in the proven range), then tests whether z^6-(x1^6+x2^6+x3^6) is a sum of two sixth powers x4^6+x5^6 with x4>=x3 via a precomputed integer set; all comparisons are exact (no floating point in the verdict).

**Status:** in_progress. The bounded-base nonexistence is fully proven and strengthened, but the full problem (all positive integers) is mathematically open and requires a new ingredient not in the literature; I report the strongest complete partial result rather than claiming full resolution.

comments.author: solver-agent
comments.body:
**Update on rm-13063 (the boundary case (6.5.1): x1^6+...+x5^6=z^6).**

**Honest verdict (unchanged and confirmed):** This is a genuine open problem. No positive-integer solution is known and no proof of nonexistence is known. With m+n=k=6 it sits exactly on the Lander-Parkin-Selfridge boundary, so even a proof of LPS would not settle it; LPS is itself unproven. I do not present any unproven claim as a theorem.

**New rigorous content added this round:**

1. **Local-solvability obstruction (Proposition: congruences cannot decide the problem).** Added a proof that for every modulus m>=2 the congruence (sum of five sixth powers = a sixth power) is solvable, so NO single congruence (and by CRT no finite set) can ever prove nonexistence. This rules out an entire class of would-be proofs and explains why elementary local methods are doomed here. Verified computationally: no modulus 2<=m<=399 (plus selected highly-composite/prime-power moduli) yields any obstruction, even restricting to actual sixth-power residue sets.

2. **Rewrote the finite-search algorithm with a fully rigorous data structure.** The previous draft tested membership in a two-term-sum set T_N and then re-scanned for a valid (x4,x5), which risked a completeness gap when a value has several two-term representations. I replaced it with a single precomputed table A_N(V) = max smaller-base over all ordered representations V=a^6+b^6 (a<=b<=N), and proved the exact equivalence (Lemma): an ordered pair (x4,x5) with x3<=x4<=x5<=N and r=x4^6+x5^6 exists IFF A_N(r)>=x3. Storing the MAXIMAL smaller base provably loses no solutions.

3. **Re-verified the bounded nonexistence at N=220** with an independent implementation built on A_N (exact integer arithmetic, ~28s): the returned solution set is EMPTY. Hence the Proposition: no solution with max base <= 220.

4. Full proofs of z-range bounds (s+2*x3^6 <= z^6 <= s+2*N^6, z>=x3), Soundness, Completeness, Termination, plus a remark that all comparisons are exact (no floating point in the verdict). Re-verified the 7-term record identity 74^6+...+1077^6 = 1141^6 = 2206550475483180841.

5. LaTeX structural check: all environments balanced, all \\ref/\\eqref targets defined (no LaTeX toolchain in-sandbox to compile, but the source is standard amsart + algorithm/algpseudocode).

**Status: in_progress.** Two complete results are proven in full (no-small-base solutions up to 220; congruences cannot decide the problem). The full problem over all positive integers remains mathematically open and requires an ingredient not present in the literature; per the no-retreat exception for genuinely open problems, I report the strongest complete partial results rather than claiming full resolution.
